source.title: Double Descent Optimization Pattern and Aliasing: Caveats of Noisy Labels
source.authors: Florian Dubost; Khaled Kamal Saab; Erin Hong; Daniel Y. Fu; M. Pike; Siddharth Sharma; Si-Yi Tang; Nandita Bhaskhar; Christopher Lee-Messer; Daniel L. Rubin

record.file_problem: The main paper text is present. Supplementary materials are referenced but not included.
record.tranche_reason: Tests epoch-wise generalization-error curves using training-time sweeps, on new datasets and networks, and reports when the fall-rise-fall pattern appears or disappears.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses model-wise and sample-wise double descent and effective model complexity in its review of prior work, but reports no own model-size sweep, sample-wise error curve, or effective-complexity test. The retained rows concern the paper's own epoch-wise results. Individual plotted learning-rate curves are not extracted separately where the text reports only aggregate outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own epoch-wise training sweeps on binary CIFAR-10 and EEG seizure forecasting. It reports whether validation loss follows a fall-rise-fall shape. Label noise, training-set size, optimizer, learning rate and sampling frequency are varied. This is T2 rather than T1: it uses binary cross-entropy validation loss, not test error, with small networks. It never checks whether training reached interpolation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that epoch-wise double descent appears when the training set is small and labels are noisy in both training and evaluation sets. It disappears at higher learning rates, possibly only hidden by aliasing from sparse sampling, and they suspect it occurs more often than reported. They also suggest the loss of the pattern with more training data may itself be an aliasing effect.
record.recipe_differences: Uses epoch-wise validation-loss curves on a binary CIFAR-10 task and a patient-wise EEG seizure-forecasting task, with Adam and Adadelta. It varies label noise, dataset size, learning rate, and sampling frequency; it also defines a polynomial-based detection procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with training-set size, whether training and validation labels are noisy, optimizer and learning rate, patient, and validation-error sampling frequency.

fits_no_version.finding: Whether epoch-wise double descent is visible depends on learning rate: it appears at small rates and is absent at intermediate ones. Sparse validation sampling can hide it through aliasing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The visibility of epoch-wise double descent depends on optimizer learning rate and on how often generalization error is sampled.

fits_no_version.finding: Noisy labels in the evaluation set are needed for the peak. Evaluation labels cannot affect training, so the peak is a property of the measured loss on noisy labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Epoch-wise loss peaks under label noise can depend on noise in the evaluation labels, not only in the training labels.

record.problems: The CIFAR-10 experiment uses a restricted binary task and a small dataset. The seizure results are patient-wise, with only nine subjects and aggregate reporting for the six, one, and two subject groups. The paper does not report numerical peak locations or uncertainty estimates. It notes that validation-set size may make generalization-error estimates unreliable and that its polynomial detection can fail when curves are undersampled.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Individual learning-rate curve values in Figures 1, 2, and 4 were not separated because the text reports aggregate outcomes and the plotted values are not stated in prose.

untested.parts: Training-set size is changed only between 300 and 3,000. Test error is not reported as a function of sample size near the interpolation threshold.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
Effective model complexity is not measured.
Multiple or triple peaks and regularization (including optimally tuned regularization) are not tested; the authors say so explicitly.
No link between the epoch-wise peak and the point where training error reaches zero; no peak heights or locations.

missing.what: At their default learning rates both optimizers converge on CIFAR-10 without double descent (results in an appendix that is not included).
Clean-label CIFAR runs are used as the reference loss for deciding that double descent has ended; no numbers are given.

record.verdict_notes: No uncertainty is reported, and the validation sets are small (300 images). Double descent is judged mainly by eye or by polynomial fitting. Runs are mostly trained longer than the figures show, and the full curves are in supplementary material that is not included.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or test-error curve over model size.
No numerical peak locations or peak heights are reported; model-size double descent is not tested.
Training-set size is changed, but the measured outcome is the epoch-wise curve, not test error as a function of sample size near an interpolation threshold.
No cross-model-class capacity sweep; cited work is not an own result.
Effective model complexity is discussed from prior work but not measured or tested.
Label-noise conditions are varied. Multiple/triple peaks and regularization, including optimally tuned regularization, are not tested.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameters or comparison to an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relation.reason: The study directly measures whether epoch-wise double descent occurs while varying dataset size, label corruption, learning rate, optimizer and validation sampling.

tranche.reason: Own experiments address epoch-wise double descent using binary classification, validation cross-entropy, polynomial-based characterization and sampling controls, supporting the different-method classification.

source_check.notes: The measured outcome is binary cross-entropy validation loss; positive CIFAR settings use corrupted evaluation labels, without establishing clean test-error curves or interpolation linkage. Figure 5 compares separate trainings; regularization is explicitly untested.

statements.correction: r6: shallow ResNet-like network; binary CIFAR-10 airplane versus ship; 300 training images; noisy training and validation labels; epoch-wise validation-loss double descent.
statements.problem: The cited r6 concerns binary CIFAR-10, whereas the statement describes unrelated forecasting, compositional and acoustic experiments. Those models and numerical trajectories are not this study's results.

statements.correction: 300 training images; noisy training labels with clean validation labels: no double descent, possible early plateau; noise in both sets: double descent; condition-specific V6 verdict: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The CIFAR-10 facts are correct, but the challenges label overstates their implication for V6: noise dependence does not assert that training-label noise alone always suffices.
